Loose
lōōs
v.t. & adj. (to unbind, to set free; rendering Hebrew pathach, nathar, Greek luō)
Saxon leas, free, unbound. The verb is the exact opposite of binding, and Scripture makes it the characteristic work of Christ upon whatever holds His people.

Biblical Definition

To loose is to undo a bond, and in Scripture the bonds Christ undoes are of four kinds. Death: “Whom God hath raised up, having loosed the pains of death: because it was not possible that he should be holden of it” (Act 2:24) — the grave could not keep its knot tied on Him. The grave-clothes of others: at Lazarus's tomb, “he that was dead came forth, bound hand and foot with graveclothes… Jesus saith unto them, Loose him, and let him go” (Joh 11:44) — Christ raises, and the church unwraps. Oppression: the fast God chooses is “to loose the bands of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens, and to let the oppressed go free, and that ye break every yoke” (Isa 58:6). And the church's declarative authority: “whatsoever thou shalt bind on earth shall be bound in heaven: and whatsoever thou shalt loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven” (Mat 16:19) — the keys of the kingdom, exercised in preaching and discipline, announcing on earth what heaven has settled. In every case the loosing is Christ's; the church is given a voice in it, never a licence over it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines loose as to untie or unbind, to free from any fastening, to relax, to release from imprisonment, and to set at liberty.

expand to see more

LOOSE, v.t. To untie or unbind; to free from any fastening.

2. To relax; as, to loose the bands of wickedness.

3. To release from imprisonment; to liberate; to set at liberty.

4. To free from obligation.

5. To disengage; to detach.

Key Scripture

Act 2:24 — "Whom God hath raised up, having loosed the pains of death: because it was not possible that he should be holden of it."

Joh 11:44 — "And he that was dead came forth, bound hand and foot with graveclothes: and his face was bound about with a napkin. Jesus saith unto them, Loose him, and let him go."

Isa 58:6 — "Is not this the fast that I have chosen? to loose the bands of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens, and to let the oppressed go free, and that ye break every yoke?"

Mat 16:19 — "And I will give unto thee the keys of the kingdom of heaven: and whatsoever thou shalt bind on earth shall be bound in heaven: and whatsoever thou shalt loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven."

Modern Corruption

Binding and loosing has been claimed as a power the church wields over heaven, and separately as a formula for commanding spirits — where the text gives a declarative authority that announces heaven's verdict rather than creating it.

expand to see more

Two claimants press on Matthew 16:19. Rome reads the keys as a jurisdiction lodged in a single office, dispensing and withholding what heaven must then ratify. Certain charismatic teachers read binding and loosing as a technique of spiritual warfare, spoken over demons, illness, or circumstances until the desired outcome is released. The Greek perfect construction points the other way in both cases: what is bound on earth shall have been bound in heaven. The church declares; heaven has already decided. The keys are the preaching of the gospel and the exercise of discipline, and they are given to the assembly, not to a technique or a throne.

Isaiah 58 keeps the doctrine from becoming abstract. The loosing God actually wants from His people is the undoing of bands His people themselves have tied — unjust burdens, withheld wages, a yoke laid on a neighbour — and He says plainly that fasting without it is worthless. A congregation confident of its authority to loose in heaven, while binding heavy burdens on the poor at its door, has read the passage exactly backwards.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew nathar (H5425), to loose or set free, and pathach (H6605), to open or unfasten; Greek luō (G3089), to loose, untie, dissolve — the verb of resurrection and of the keys.

expand to see more

Hebrew nathar (H5425) — to loose, set free; “to loose the bands of wickedness” (Isa 58:6).

Greek luō (G3089) — to loose, untie, release, dissolve; the loosed pains of death (Act 2:24) and the loosing of Mat 16:19.

The same verb is used of dissolving the works of the devil (1Jn 3:8) — Christ came to untie what Satan tied.

Usage

"“Having loosed the pains of death” — the grave could not hold its knot."

"“Loose him, and let him go” — Christ raises; the church unwraps."

"“To loose the bands of wickedness” — the fast God actually chooses."
